\section{Generalization and Robustness}
\label{sec:generalization}

The atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) established in-distribution accuracy of 69.6--85.4\%.
We now test whether these results reflect genuine statistical regularities or artifacts of specific training conditions, evaluating four axes: classifier choice (\S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}), cross-model transfer (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossmodel}), cross-strategy transfer (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}), and end-to-end learned representations (\S\ref{sec:gen:dcol}).

\subsection{Baseline Comparison}
\label{sec:gen:baselines}

Table~\ref{tab:baselines} compares classification methods on the Pythia-1.4B nucleus setting.
Three feature-based methods---Random Forest (RF), CORAL ordinal regression \cite{coral2020}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026}---all operate on the same 19 statistical features and achieve near-identical accuracy (78.1--78.2\%).
A cross-entropy MLP and logistic regression trail by $\sim$3 percentage points.
Single-feature regression on mean perplexity performs at chance (25.1\%), confirming that depth estimation requires the multi-dimensional feature representation defined in \S\ref{sec:method}.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Comparison of classification methods on Pythia-1.4B nucleus. RF, CORAL, and DivEye use the same 19 statistical features. Chance = 25\%.}
\label{tab:baselines}
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
Method & 4-class Acc (\%) \\
\midrule
RF (19 features) & \textbf{78.2} \\
CORAL & 78.1 \\
DivEye & 78.2 \\
CE-MLP & 74.9 \\
LR & 75.0 \\
DeepSeek V3.2 (zero-shot) & 44.3 \\
ppl-regression (single feature) & 25.1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The convergence of RF, CORAL, and DivEye indicates that the discriminative signal resides in the features, not the classifier.
Across all 9 atlas cells, RF $\geq$ CORAL $>$ DivEye $>$ LR, with a maximum gap of $\sim$4 percentage points.
A zero-shot LLM baseline (DeepSeek V3.2) achieves 44.3\% on 200 samples---above chance but 34 points below feature-based methods, suggesting that depth estimation from raw text requires explicit statistical computation rather than general language understanding.

Figure~\ref{fig:confusion_matrix} shows confusion matrices for the best and worst atlas cells.
In both cases, d0 (human text) is near-perfectly identified, while errors concentrate at the d1--d2 boundary---a pattern we revisit in \S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{../../figures/paper/fig_confusion_matrix.pdf}
\caption{Confusion matrices for the best (GPT-2 XL, temp $\tau{=}0.9$, 85.4\%) and worst (Pythia-1.4B, top-$k$ $k{=}50$, 69.6\%) in-distribution settings. d0 recall exceeds 98\% in both; errors concentrate at the d1/d2 boundary.}
\label{fig:confusion_matrix}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:gen:crossmodel}

To test whether depth fingerprints generalize across architectures, we perform leave-one-model-family-out evaluation: train on two model families (nucleus sampling only) and test on the held-out third.
Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} reports results.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-model transfer (leave-one-out, nucleus only). Train on 2 model families, test on held-out 3rd. Chance = 25\%.}
\label{tab:cross_model}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Holdout & Acc & d0 & d1 & d2 & d3 \\
 & (\%) & Rec. & Rec. & Rec. & Rec. \\
\midrule
Pythia & 62.4 & 100.0 & 49.3 & 26.8 & 73.6 \\
OLMo & \textbf{69.2} & 99.3 & 75.5 & 43.3 & 58.8 \\
GPT-2 XL & 67.6 & 98.5 & 74.7 & 52.6 & 44.5 \\
\midrule
Mean & 66.4 & 99.3 & 66.5 & 40.9 & 59.0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Mean transfer accuracy reaches 66.4\%, well above chance (2.7$\times$) and the 45\% transfer gate.
The per-class breakdown reveals that d0 recall ($>$98\%) inflates headline accuracy; the real challenge lies in distinguishing machine-generated depths from each other.
d2 recall drops as low as 26.8\% when Pythia is held out, making it the most confusable depth class.
Pythia is the hardest holdout overall (62.4\%), while OLMo is the easiest (69.2\%)---a 6.8 percentage point spread across model families.

\subsection{Cross-Strategy Transfer}
\label{sec:gen:crossstrategy}

We next train on two decoding strategies and test on the held-out third.
Table~\ref{tab:cross_strategy} reports per-model results.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-strategy transfer (leave-one-out). Train on 2 strategies, test on held-out 3rd. Chance = 25\%.}
\label{tab:cross_strategy}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
Holdout & Pythia & OLMo & GPT-2 XL \\
 & Acc (\%) & Acc (\%) & Acc (\%) \\
\midrule
nucleus & \textbf{69.4} & \textbf{65.4} & \textbf{59.9} \\
temp ($\tau{=}0.9$) & 62.8 & 58.2 & 56.1 \\
top-$k$ ($k{=}50$) & 51.5 & 54.9 & 53.6 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Mean cross-strategy accuracy (59.1\%) falls 7 points below cross-model transfer (66.4\%), indicating that strategy-induced distribution shifts pose a greater generalization challenge than architectural differences.

\paragraph{Temperature-induced boundary inversion.}
The most striking finding emerges from the d1-vs-d2 binary AUC when temperature sampling is held out.
Training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1v2 AUC of 0.129 for GPT-2~XL and 0.253 for OLMo---both below 0.5, indicating that the classifier's d1/d2 decision boundary \emph{inverts} under temperature sampling.
Only Pythia retains a degraded but non-inverted AUC of 0.576.

This inversion is predicted by the trajectory analysis in \S\ref{sec:atlas}: temperature sampling accelerates convergence toward the low-entropy attractor, shifting feature values at depth $d$ to resemble depth $d{+}1$ under nucleus or top-$k$.
A classifier trained on the latter two strategies therefore learns a d1/d2 boundary that, when applied to temperature-sampled text, falls on the wrong side of the shifted distributions---samples the classifier labels as d1 are actually d2 and vice versa.

\paragraph{Z-score normalization does not resolve the inversion.}
A natural hypothesis is that per-feature z-score normalization might correct this covariate shift \cite{sugiyama2007}.
We test this and find that z-normalization leaves RF accuracy essentially unchanged (59.1\% $\to$ 59.2\%) and does not improve d1v2 AUC ($\Delta < 0.02$).
This null result is expected: RF splits depend on feature rank order, not scale, making them invariant to monotonic transforms.
A separate experiment with logistic regression reveals that z-normalization \emph{does} recover d1v2 AUC from 0.13 to 0.68, confirming a two-layer structure in the distribution shift: (1)~a scale component correctable by linear normalization that helps parametric classifiers, and (2)~a feature-space geometry component that is tree-invariant and that z-normalization cannot address.
The temperature covariate shift is therefore not merely a calibration problem but a structural rearrangement of the feature space.

\subsection{End-to-End Learning: A Negative Result}
\label{sec:gen:dcol}

Given the success of hand-crafted features, we investigate whether end-to-end learning can bypass feature engineering.
We implement Deep Contrastive Ordinal Learning (DCOL) with a RoBERTa-large encoder and ordinal contrastive loss, training directly on raw text passages.

Across six configurations (v1--v6), DCOL fails to match feature-based methods.
Versions v1--v3 suffer embedding collapse; v4 triggers out-of-memory errors; v5 produces NaN losses.
The best run (v6) reaches test accuracy of 64.5\%---13.7 points below RF (78.2\%)---with severe overfitting: training accuracy reaches 75\% versus validation accuracy of 64.4\% at the best epoch (epoch 1), and early stopping triggers by epoch 4.

This negative result suggests that the 19-dimensional statistical summary defined in \S\ref{sec:method} captures depth-relevant information that a transformer encoder struggles to extract from raw token sequences.
The features encode explicit tail behavior (percentile perplexities) and distributional shape (surprisal variance, entropy)---second-order statistics of the token distribution that may require substantially more data for a neural network to learn implicitly.

## Section Structure (word budget: 1000 words)

```
\section{Task Formulation}
\label{sec:method}

§3.1 Problem Definition
§3.2 Multi-Generational Benchmark Construction
§3.3 Statistical Feature Design
§3.4 Effective Discriminable Depth (EDD)
```

## DATA

### §3.1 Problem Definition
- Given text x, estimate recursive generation depth d ∈ {0, 1, ..., K}
  - d=0: human-written seed text
  - d=k (k≥1): text generated by model finetuned on depth-(k-1) data
- This is an ordinal classification problem: d=1 is "closer" to d=0 than d=3

### §3.2 Multi-Generational Benchmark Construction
- 3 model families: Pythia-1.4B (EleutherAI), OLMo-1B (AI2), GPT-2 XL (OpenAI, 1.5B)
  - All 1-1.5B scale, diverse architectures
- 3 decoding strategies: nucleus sampling (p=0.95), temperature sampling (τ=0.9), top-k sampling (k=50)
- 4 depths (d0-d3) for main atlas, extended to d0-d5 for depth extension experiments
- 5,000 samples per depth per cell → total 180K samples across 9 cells × 4 depths
- Pipeline: seed text (Wikipedia subset) → LoRA finetune (r=16, α=32, 3 epochs, lr=2e-4, batch=8) → generate (max 512 tokens) → repeat
- LoRA modules: c_attn + c_proj (GPT-2 family), q_proj + v_proj (OLMo)
- Reference model: GPT-2 base (124M), independent of generation models
  - Computes per-token perplexity on each text passage
  - Cross-model LOO: reference model stays fixed (does not change when holding out GPT-2 XL — partial overlap discussed in §6)

### §3.3 Statistical Feature Design (tab_features)
19-dimensional feature vector f(x) extracted from reference-model perplexity distribution:

**Perplexity statistics (9 features):**
- mean_ppl, var_ppl: mean and variance of per-token perplexity
- skewness_ppl, kurtosis_ppl: shape statistics
- p10_ppl, p25_ppl, p50_ppl, p75_ppl, p90_ppl: percentile quantiles

**Surprisal statistics (3 features):**
- mean_surprisal, var_surprisal: mean and variance of -log p(token)
- entropy_of_surprisal: entropy of the surprisal distribution

**Lexical diversity (3 features):**
- type_token_ratio: unique tokens / total tokens
- hapax_ratio: tokens appearing exactly once / total
- bigram_entropy, trigram_entropy: n-gram diversity

**Repetition (3 features):**
- rep_2gram, rep_3gram, rep_4gram: fraction of repeated n-grams

Note: The 19 features should be presented in a compact table (tab_features). If space is tight, move to appendix and just describe the categories in text.

### §3.4 Effective Discriminable Depth (EDD)
- Definition: EDD_T = max d* such that AUC(d*, d*+1) ≥ T
  - Uses dedicated binary RF per adjacent depth pair
  - Default threshold T=0.75, sensitivity analysis at T ∈ {0.65, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80}
- AUC measured as one-vs-one binary classification between adjacent depths
- EDD captures: "how deep can we reliably distinguish?"
- RF: 200 trees for 4-class, 500 trees for binary pairwise (increased for convergence on smaller samples)

### Classifiers
- Primary: Random Forest (200 trees, max_depth=None, 5-fold stratified CV)
- Baselines: CORAL ordinal regression, DivEye (surprisal diversity), CE-MLP (2-layer, cross-entropy), Logistic Regression
- Lower bound: single-feature ppl regression (mean_ppl only → chance-level 25.1%)

- d: recursive generation depth (d=0 human-written)
- K: maximum depth in benchmark (K=3 for atlas, K=5 for extension)
- EDD_T: Effective Discriminable Depth at AUC threshold T
- f(x): 19-dim statistical feature vector
- M = {Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2 XL}: model families
- S = {nucleus p=0.95, temp τ=0.9, top-k k=50}: decoding strategies

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical---it is already occurring in the wild---yet we lack the ability to determine how many recursive iterations a given text has undergone, a distinction that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all generation depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
Watermarking schemes \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} require proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively to existing corpora.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} characterizes how recursive training degrades model quality but assumes the generation depth is known a priori---the very quantity we seek to estimate.
\citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} show that filtering synthetic data from training corpora can prevent collapse, yet their approach relies on binary detection and does not distinguish among recursive depths.
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates the extent of single-pass editing applied to a text but does not address multi-step recursive generation.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive depth of a text passage from its content alone.

Our key insight is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints exhibit universal stability across model families and decoding strategies.
Specifically, perplexity tail statistics---the 90th-percentile perplexity (\textsc{p90\_ppl}) and surprisal variance (\textsc{var\_surprisal})---emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by Gini importance in 9/9 and 7/9 model--strategy configurations, respectively.

We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as an ordinal classification task and introduce a lightweight pipeline to solve it.
Given a text passage, we compute a 19-dimensional feature vector from reference-model perplexity statistics---capturing distributional location, spread, tail behavior, and lexical diversity---and classify it with a Random Forest into one of $K{+}1$ depth classes ($d{=}0$ for human text through $d{=}K$ for $K$-th generation text).
To systematically characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and decoding strategies (nucleus $p{=}0.95$, temperature $\tau{=}0.9$, top-$k$ $k{=}50$), each spanning 4 generation depths, totaling 180K samples.
The atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories---temperature sampling accelerates convergence toward a low-entropy attractor, while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---and we introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.

Our contributions are:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Task formalization.} We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification, distinguishing it from binary detection and single-pass editing estimation. We introduce the EDD metric, which summarizes the maximum depth at which adjacent generations remain separable above a given AUC threshold.

    \item \textbf{Depth Degradation Atlas.} We construct a systematic $3 \times 3$ map across model families and decoding strategies, revealing that \textsc{p90\_ppl} ranks in the top 2 in all 9 cells (100\%) and \textsc{var\_surprisal} in 7/9 (78\%), with a mean Spearman rank correlation of $\rho{=}0.868$ across importance vectors. The extended Pythia nucleus pipeline (d0--d5) yields $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$, establishing that depth discrimination persists through four recursive steps before falling below threshold.

    \item \textbf{Generalization analysis.} Cross-model leave-one-out transfer achieves 66.4\% mean accuracy and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\% (chance = 25\%), demonstrating partial universality of depth fingerprints. We identify a temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion (GPT-2~XL: 0.13, OLMo: 0.25) caused by accelerated convergence, and show that z-score normalization does not resolve this structural covariate shift for tree-based classifiers.

    \item \textbf{End-to-end learning as negative result.} Deep Contrastive Ordinal Learning (DCOL) with RoBERTa-large, tested across 6 configurations, achieves at best 64.5\% versus 78.2\% for RF on the same data, with 5 of 6 runs failing due to embedding collapse, OOM, or NaN losses. This suggests that explicit statistical features capture depth-relevant information that end-to-end models struggle to extract from raw text.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
\citet{shumailov2024_nature} demonstrate that recursively training language models on their own outputs erodes distributional tails, eventually collapsing the output distribution to a narrow mode.
\citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} formalize this phenomenon through scaling laws that distinguish tail \emph{narrowing} (reduced variance) from tail \emph{cutting} (lost support), showing both accelerate with recursion depth.
The MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad} extends this analysis to self-consuming generative models and quantifies the precision--recall tradeoff as synthetic data accumulates across generations.
\citet{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate} show that retaining real data alongside synthetic data across generations mitigates collapse, while \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} demonstrate that filtering synthetic samples via binary detection can preserve model quality.
Recent work further refines the theoretical picture: \citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} identify non-monotonic dynamics where early recursion can temporarily \emph{improve} model quality before eventual degradation; \citet{marchi2024_heat_death} characterize convergence to a fixed-point ``heat death'' distribution; and \citet{wang2026_contamination} derive contamination guarantees bounding how much synthetic data a corpus can absorb.
Additional lines of work address curated synthetic pipelines \cite{falahati2026_curated}, knowledge collapse in factual recall \cite{knowledge_collapse2025}, spectral signatures of model-generated text \cite{sigma2026_spectral}, and the ``synthetic eggs'' problem in self-improving loops \cite{synthetic_eggs2026}.
These works characterize degradation patterns but assume the generation depth is known a priori; our work addresses the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.

\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}
DetectGPT \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt} introduced probability curvature---the tendency of model-generated text to occupy local maxima of the log-probability surface---as a zero-shot detection signal.
\citet{fast_detectgpt2024} improve computational efficiency by replacing random perturbations with conditional probability curvature from a surrogate model.
Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024} exploits the perplexity ratio between two related models, achieving strong detection without training data.
DivEye \cite{diveye2026} leverages surprisal diversity patterns, while GLTR \cite{gehrmann2019_gltr} provides statistical visualization of per-token likelihood ranks for human inspection.
\citet{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} expose fundamental limits: paraphrasing attacks reduce detection accuracy to near chance, and \citet{pudasaini2026_detection_fails} show detection degrades under distribution shift between training and deployment domains.
\citet{pu2026_generator_barrier} formalize a generator barrier bounding detection performance when the generator is unknown.
All these methods perform binary classification (human vs.\ machine), discarding the ordinal depth information that distinguishes first-generation from deeply recursive text.
Our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing binary detection.

\paragraph{Adjacent Tasks.}
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates the \emph{extent} of editing applied to a passage---a continuous measure of how much a text has been modified in a single pass---but does not model recursive generation chains.
\citet{uchendu2020_attribution} formulate authorship attribution as multi-source classification, identifying \emph{which} model generated a text rather than \emph{how many} recursive steps it has undergone.
LOKI \cite{loki2025} provides a comprehensive benchmark spanning multiple synthetic data modalities but evaluates binary detection, not depth estimation.
These tasks probe complementary dimensions of synthetic text characterization; none estimates recursive depth.

\paragraph{Decoding Strategy Effects.}
The choice of decoding strategy shapes the statistical properties of generated text in ways that interact with recursive depth signals.
\citet{holtzman2020_nucleus} show that unrestricted sampling produces degenerate repetitions and propose nucleus sampling to maintain output diversity.
\citet{finlayson2024_closing} demonstrate that decoding parameters affect downstream evaluation metrics in non-trivial ways.
\citet{garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded} find that the effect of decoding strategies on text quality is model-dependent, complicating universal quality claims.
\citet{wiher2022_decoding} provide a systematic comparison of decoding methods on surface-level text properties, and Mirostat \cite{basu2021_mirostat} introduces perplexity-controlled decoding that actively regulates output entropy.
Our Depth Degradation Atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) reveals that these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation---temperature sampling accelerates convergence to a low-entropy attractor while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---effects that go beyond single-pass text quality to shape the discriminability of recursive depth itself.
